course.title: Game Development with Unity
course.tagline: Build and publish your first 2D game with Unity and C#, from idea to playable build.

days.title: What Game Development Is and Installing Unity
days.goal: Understand what game development is and install Unity on your computer.

video.title: The Unity Tutorial For Complete Beginners

steps: Go to unity.com, download Unity Hub and install it.
In Unity Hub, install the latest LTS version of the Unity Editor.
Add the Android and WebGL build modules if you have space.
Open Unity Hub and check the Editor is listed and ready.
days.task: Install Unity Hub and the Unity Editor, then open Unity Hub.
days.challenge: Write down the Unity version you installed.

options: A game engine: software for building 2D and 3D games
quiz.explain: Unity is a game engine. It gives you the tools to build, test and publish games.

options: The app that installs and manages Unity Editors and your projects
quiz.explain: Unity Hub installs Unity versions and keeps your projects in one place.

options: A long-term support version: stable and supported for two years
quiz.explain: LTS means long-term support. It is the stable version, best for learning and for real projects.

days.title: Your First Unity Project
days.goal: Create a project and learn your way around the Unity Editor.

video.title: Unity for Beginners: Build Your First Game From Zero

steps: Create a new 2D project in Unity Hub and name it MyFirstGame.
Open the project and find the five main windows: Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project and Inspector.
Click around each window and see what it shows.
Save the scene with Ctrl+S or Cmd+S.
days.task: Create your first 2D project and save the scene.
days.challenge: Write down what each of the five main windows does.

options: The game as players see it
The editor view where you build and arrange your game world
quiz.explain: The Scene window is your workshop. You place and move objects there to build your game.

options: A preview of what players will see when the game runs
quiz.explain: The Game window shows the game as players see it. Press Play to see it run.

options: A list of every object currently in your scene
quiz.explain: The Hierarchy lists all the objects in your scene, in a tree you can expand and collapse.

days.title: GameObjects, Components and the Inspector
days.goal: Understand GameObjects and add components to them.

video.title: How to Make a Game! Download and Create New Project

steps: Create an empty GameObject in the Hierarchy.
Add a Sprite Renderer component to it.
Give it a simple sprite, like a square, and see it appear in the Scene.
Change its position, rotation and scale in the Inspector.
days.task: Make a scene with three objects: a square, a circle and a triangle, each a different colour.
days.challenge: Move, rotate and scale each one with the Inspector.

options: Anything in your scene: a character, a platform, a light, a camera
quiz.explain: A GameObject is any object in your scene. Everything in a Unity game is a GameObject.

options: A piece of behaviour or data attached to a GameObject, like a Sprite Renderer or a Rigidbody
quiz.explain: Components give GameObjects abilities. A Sprite Renderer draws it, a Rigidbody gives it physics.

options: It shows the selected object's components so you can change them
quiz.explain: The Inspector shows everything about the object you selected, and lets you change its values.

days.title: C# Basics for Unity
days.goal: Learn the C# you need for Unity: variables, methods and classes.

video.title: Complete C# Programming

steps: Learn what a variable is and make one for health and one for speed.
Write a method called TakeDamage that reduces health by a number.
Learn the difference between int, float and string.
Write a simple class for a player with health and a name.
days.task: Write a C# script with variables for a player's name, health and speed.
days.challenge: Write a method that heals the player by 10 points.

options: The programming language Unity uses for game code
quiz.explain: C# is the language you write Unity game code in. Scripts are C# files attached to GameObjects.

options: A named box that stores a value you can use and change
quiz.explain: A variable is a name that stores a value, like health = 100, which your code can read and change.

options: A block of code that does one job and can be called by name
quiz.explain: A method is a named piece of code that does one job, like TakeDamage() or Jump().

days.title: Your First Script: Moving a Character
days.goal: Write a script that moves a character with the keyboard.

video.title: How to Make Wall Slide in a 2D Game in Unity for Beginners

steps: Create a C# script called PlayerMovement and attach it to your square.
In Update(), read Input.GetAxis('Horizontal') to get left and right input.
Move the character by changing its position each frame.
Press Play and move your character with the arrow keys or A and D.
days.task: Make a character that moves left and right with the arrow keys.
days.challenge: Make the character move faster by changing the speed value.

options: A method Unity calls once every frame
quiz.explain: Update() runs every frame. Code in it, like movement, happens continuously while the game runs.

options: A number from -1 to 1 based on left and right keys
quiz.explain: GetAxis returns -1 for left, 1 for right, and 0 when no key is pressed. It is smooth, not just on or off.

options: So movement is the same speed on fast and slow computers
quiz.explain: deltaTime is the time since the last frame. Multiplying by it makes movement frame-rate independent.

days.title: Physics: Gravity and Collisions
days.goal: Add physics so your character falls, lands and bumps into things.

video.title: How to make a 2D Game in Unity

steps: Add a Rigidbody2D to your character so gravity pulls it down.
Add a BoxCollider2D to your character and to the ground.
Press Play and watch the character fall and land on the ground.
Change the gravity scale and see the fall get faster or slower.
days.task: Make a character that falls onto a platform and stays there.
days.challenge: Add a second platform and a wall, and check the character collides with both.

options: A component that gives an object physics: gravity, velocity and forces
quiz.explain: A Rigidbody2D makes an object obey physics. Gravity pulls it, forces push it, and it collides with other objects.

options: An invisible shape that defines where an object can be touched or hit
quiz.explain: A collider is the object's physical shape. Unity uses it to detect touches and bumps.

options: Other objects pass straight through it
quiz.explain: Without a collider, an object has no physical presence. Other objects pass through it.

days.title: Project 1: Simple Platformer Level
days.goal: Build a small platformer level with a character that runs and jumps.

video.title: 2D Camera in Unity (Cinemachine Tutorial)

steps: Build a level with a ground and at least five platforms.
Add a character with movement, jumping and gravity.
Add a goal flag at the end of the level.
Play the level from start to finish and fix anything that feels wrong.
days.task: Finish the platformer level and play it through to the goal.
days.challenge: Add a pit that the player must jump over.

quiz.q: What makes a good first level?
options: A clear path, easy jumps first, and one goal at the end
quiz.explain: A good first level teaches the player: easy jumps, a clear route, and a goal that is easy to see.

quiz.q: Why test your level by playing it?
options: Because you only find bad jumps and unfair spots by playing
quiz.explain: Playing reveals problems you cannot see in the editor: jumps that are too far, platforms that are too small.

quiz.q: What is a jump in code?
options: Giving the character an upward velocity when the jump button is pressed and it is on the ground
quiz.explain: A jump sets the character's upward speed for a moment. Gravity then brings it back down.

project.title: Simple Platformer Level
project.brief: Build a small platformer level in Unity: a ground and at least five platforms, a character that runs and jumps with gravity, and a goal flag at the end. Play the level from start to finish.
checks: The level has a ground and at least five platforms.
The character moves left and right with the keyboard.
The character can jump and lands on platforms.
A goal flag marks the end of the level.
The level can be played from start to finish.
The game runs without errors.

days.title: Jumping and Ground Detection
days.goal: Make jumping feel good with proper ground checks.

video.title: How to Make a Video Game in Unity – Programming (E02)

steps: Add a ground check: a small circle under the character that tests if it touches the ground.
Only allow jumping when the character is grounded.
Add coyote time: let the player jump for a short moment after leaving a ledge.
Tune the jump force until it feels right.
days.task: Make your jump feel good: test it ten times and adjust the force.
days.challenge: Add a double jump and test it.

quiz.q: Why check if the character is grounded?
options: So the player cannot jump in mid-air forever
quiz.explain: Without a ground check, the player can jump again and again in the air, which breaks the game.

options: A short grace period after leaving a ledge when jumping still works
quiz.explain: Coyote time forgives a late jump by a fraction of a second, which makes the game feel fair and responsive.

options: Because the right force makes jumps feel good: not too floaty, not too heavy
quiz.explain: Jump feel is the heart of a platformer. Small changes in force change how the whole game feels.

days.title: Collectables and Score
days.goal: Add coins to collect and a score that goes up.

video.title: Learn C# Beginner FREE Tutorial Course!

steps: Make a coin GameObject with a sprite and a trigger collider.
Write a script that adds 1 to the score when the player touches a coin.
Destroy the coin when it is collected.
Show the score on the screen with a UI Text element.
days.task: Add ten coins to your level and a score display.
days.challenge: Add a sound or a sparkle effect when a coin is collected.

options: A collider that detects when something enters it, without blocking movement
quiz.explain: A trigger collider does not block. It calls a function when something enters it, which is perfect for pickups.

options: A method Unity calls when another collider enters this trigger
quiz.explain: OnTriggerEnter2D runs when something enters the trigger. You put your pickup code there.

quiz.q: How do you show the score on screen?
options: With a UI Text element that your script updates
quiz.explain: A UI Text element shows the score. Your script changes its text whenever the score changes.

days.title: Enemies and Hazards
days.goal: Add enemies that move and hazards that hurt the player.

video.title: COMPLETE COURSE - 2D Game Development in Unity (FREE)

steps: Make an enemy that walks back and forth between two points.
Make the player lose health when it touches an enemy.
Add spikes that damage the player on touch.
Add a short invincibility time after taking damage so the player is not hit twice at once.
days.task: Add two enemies and a spike trap to your level.
days.challenge: Make the enemy turn around at the edge of its platform.

options: It moves in one direction until it hits a wall or an edge, then turns around
quiz.explain: A patrolling enemy walks one way, then turns when it reaches a wall or an edge, and walks back.

quiz.q: Why add invincibility time after damage?
options: So one touch does not take all the player's health in a single second
quiz.explain: Without a short grace period, one touch can trigger many hits in a row and kill the player instantly.

options: Something in the level that hurts the player, like spikes or lava
quiz.explain: Hazards are level dangers. They damage the player on touch and make the level challenging.

days.title: Health, Damage and Death
days.goal: Handle player health, death and respawning.

video.title: The Unity Tutorial For Complete Beginners

steps: Add a health value to the player and a health bar on the screen.
Reduce health when the player is hurt and update the bar.
When health reaches zero, show a 'Game Over' screen.
Add a restart button that reloads the level.
days.task: Add a health bar and a game over screen to your level.
days.challenge: Make the player respawn at the start after falling into a pit.

options: A UI element that shows how much health the player has left
quiz.explain: A health bar is a UI element, often a filled bar, that shows the player's remaining health at a glance.

options: Bringing the player back at a safe point after dying
quiz.explain: Respawning puts the player back at a checkpoint or the start, so they can try again without restarting everything.

quiz.q: Why show a game over screen?
options: So the player knows the run ended and can choose to try again
quiz.explain: A game over screen explains what happened and offers a clear next step: try again.

days.title: Camera: Following the Player
days.goal: Make the camera follow the player smoothly.

video.title: Unity for Beginners: Build Your First Game From Zero

steps: Write a script that moves the camera to the player's position each frame.
Add smoothing so the camera glides instead of snapping.
Clamp the camera so it does not show outside the level.
Test it by running through the level.
days.task: Add a smooth following camera to your level.
days.challenge: Make the camera look slightly ahead in the direction the player moves.

quiz.q: Why does the camera need to follow the player?
options: Because the level is bigger than the screen, and the player must always be visible
quiz.explain: The camera shows only part of the level. It must follow the player so the action stays on screen.

options: Moving the camera gradually toward the player instead of snapping to them
quiz.explain: Smoothing moves the camera a little each frame toward its target, which feels gentle instead of jerky.

options: So it never shows the empty space outside the level
quiz.explain: Clamping limits the camera's position so it stays inside the level and never shows the void beyond it.

days.title: Cinemachine: Better Cameras
days.goal: Use Cinemachine for professional camera work.

video.title: How to Make a Game! Download and Create New Project

steps: Install the Cinemachine package from the Package Manager.
Add a Cinemachine Virtual Camera to your scene.
Set the player as the Follow target.
Adjust the dead zone so the camera only moves when the player leaves the centre.
days.task: Replace your camera script with a Cinemachine virtual camera.
days.challenge: Add a second virtual camera for a boss area and switch to it.

options: Unity's camera system that handles following, framing and transitions for you
quiz.explain: Cinemachine is Unity's camera tool. You set a target and rules, and it moves the camera smoothly for you.

options: A Cinemachine camera that controls the real camera's position and settings
quiz.explain: A virtual camera is a set of camera instructions. The real camera follows whichever virtual camera is active.

options: An area in the centre where the player can move without the camera following
quiz.explain: A dead zone is the middle of the screen where the player moves freely. The camera only moves when they leave it.

days.title: Project 2: Complete 2D Platformer
days.goal: Build a complete 2D platformer with levels, enemies, coins and menus.

video.title: Complete C# Programming

steps: Plan the game: three levels, enemies, coins, a goal and a main menu.
Build the levels with platforms, hazards and collectables.
Add a score, health, game over and win screens.
Play the whole game from the menu to the final level.
days.task: Finish the platformer and play it from start to finish.
days.challenge: Ask one person to play it and write down what confused them.

options: A menu, playable levels, a goal, win and lose states, and no crashes
quiz.explain: A complete game has a start, a middle and an end: menu, levels, win and lose, and it runs without breaking.

options: Because you know your game too well to see what confuses a new player
quiz.explain: You know where everything is. A new player shows you what is unclear, unfair or broken.

quiz.q: What should you do with playtest feedback?
options: Fix the biggest problems first, then test again
quiz.explain: Fix the biggest problems first. Small polish can wait until the game works well.

project.title: Complete 2D Platformer
project.brief: Build a complete 2D platformer: three levels, enemies, coins, a score and health, a main menu, game over and win screens. Play the whole game from the menu to the final level.
checks: The game has three levels.
Enemies and coins exist in the levels.
A score and health bar show on screen.
A main menu, game over and win screens exist.
The game can be played from the menu to the final level.
The game runs without errors.

days.title: UI: Menus, Buttons and HUD
days.goal: Build menus and a HUD with Unity's UI system.

video.title: How to Make Wall Slide in a 2D Game in Unity for Beginners

steps: Make a Canvas and add a main menu with a title and a Play button.
Make the Play button load your level when clicked.
Add a pause menu that appears when you press Escape.
Add a HUD with the score and health bar.
days.task: Build a main menu, a pause menu and a HUD for your game.
days.challenge: Make the Play button start the level and the Quit button close the game.

options: The area that holds all UI elements like text, buttons and images
quiz.explain: A Canvas is the parent for UI. All buttons, text and images live on a Canvas.

options: Heads-up display: the score, health and other info shown during play
quiz.explain: The HUD is the information on screen during play: score, health, lives and timers.

quiz.q: How does a button work in Unity?
options: A Button component calls a method you choose when it is clicked
quiz.explain: A Button has an onClick event. You link it to a method, and clicking runs that method.

days.title: Sound and Music
days.goal: Add sound effects and music to your game.

video.title: How to make a 2D Game in Unity

steps: Add an AudioSource to your player and a jump sound to it.
Play a sound when a coin is collected.
Add background music that loops on the menu and in levels.
Add a mute button to the pause menu.
days.task: Add jump, coin and hurt sounds to your game, plus background music.
days.challenge: Test the game with sound on and off.

options: A component that plays a sound from a GameObject
quiz.explain: An AudioSource plays a sound clip. You attach it to a GameObject and tell it which clip to play.

options: A sound file, like a jump or a coin sound
quiz.explain: An AudioClip is the sound file itself. An AudioSource plays it.

quiz.q: Why add sound to a game?
options: Because sound gives feedback: jumps, coins and hits feel real
quiz.explain: Sound tells the player what happened: a coin sound confirms the pickup, a hurt sound warns of danger.

days.title: Animations: Sprites and Animator
days.goal: Animate your character with sprite animations.

video.title: 2D Camera in Unity (Cinemachine Tutorial)

steps: Make a sprite sheet with frames for idle, run and jump.
Slice the sprite sheet in Unity and make animation clips.
Set up an Animator Controller with states for idle, run and jump.
Switch states based on the character's speed and whether it is grounded.
days.task: Animate your character: idle when still, run when moving, jump when in the air.
days.challenge: Add a hurt animation that plays when the player takes damage.

options: One image that holds many animation frames in a grid
quiz.explain: A sprite sheet packs many frames into one image. Unity slices it into separate frames for animation.

options: A state machine that decides which animation plays and when to switch
quiz.explain: The Animator Controller holds your animations as states and the rules for moving between them.

options: A rule that says when to switch from one animation to another
quiz.explain: A transition links two animation states with a condition, like 'speed is greater than 0'.

days.title: Particles and Juice
days.goal: Add particles and small effects that make the game feel alive.

video.title: How to Make a Video Game in Unity – Programming (E02)

steps: Add a particle system for dust when the player lands.
Add a burst of particles when a coin is collected.
Add a screen shake when the player takes damage.
Add a squash and stretch effect when the player jumps and lands.
days.task: Add particles to your game: dust on landing, a burst on coins, and a shake on damage.
days.challenge: Ask one person if the game feels better with the effects.

options: Many small images that move and fade, used for dust, sparks, smoke and magic
quiz.explain: Particles are tiny sprites that spawn, move and fade. They make effects like dust, explosions and sparkles.

options: Small effects like particles, shake and squash that make a game feel good
quiz.explain: Juice is the small stuff that makes a game feel alive: particles, sounds, shake and squash. It turns a plain game into a fun one.

options: Because a small shake makes hits feel powerful and alerts the player
quiz.explain: A tiny shake on damage makes the hit feel real and grabs the player's attention.

days.title: Level Design Basics
days.goal: Design levels that teach, challenge and reward the player.

video.title: Learn C# Beginner FREE Tutorial Course!

steps: Learn the three rules: teach one thing at a time, make it fair, reward the player.
Sketch your next level on paper before building it in Unity.
Place coins to guide the player toward the goal.
Test the level with a friend and watch where they get stuck.
days.task: Design a new level on paper, then build it in Unity.
days.challenge: Move the coins to guide the player along the intended path.

options: Planning where platforms, enemies, coins and goals go so the level is fun and fair
quiz.explain: Level design is arranging the pieces of a level so it teaches, challenges and rewards the player.

quiz.q: Why place coins along the path?
options: Because coins guide the player toward the goal and reward exploring
quiz.explain: Coins act as breadcrumbs. Players follow them, which leads them along the path you designed.

options: Hidden dangers, jumps that are impossible, or rules the player was never taught
quiz.explain: A fair level teaches before it tests. An unfair level punishes the player for things they could not know.

days.title: Saving and Loading Progress
days.goal: Save the player's progress so it survives closing the game.

video.title: COMPLETE COURSE - 2D Game Development in Unity (FREE)

steps: Use PlayerPrefs to save the highest level reached.
Save the player's coin total and best score.
Load the saved values when the game starts.
Add a reset button that clears the save.
days.task: Save the player's progress and best score, and load them on start.
days.challenge: Test it: play, close the game, open it again and check the save is there.

options: Unity's simple way to save small values like scores and settings
quiz.explain: PlayerPrefs saves small values on the device, like high scores and settings, so they survive closing the game.

options: So players do not lose everything when they close the game
quiz.explain: Saving lets players continue where they left off. Without it, every session starts from zero.

options: Progress, scores, settings and unlocks: small values that matter to the player
quiz.explain: Save what matters: the level reached, the best score, settings and unlocks. Save files can grow too big if you save everything.

days.title: Project 3: Your Own Game
days.goal: Design and build your own 2D game from scratch.

video.title: The Unity Tutorial For Complete Beginners

steps: Pick a game idea and write a one-page design: goal, controls, enemies, win and lose.
Build the game in Unity with at least three levels or a score chase.
Add sound, particles and a main menu.
Playtest it with two people and fix the top problems.
days.task: Finish your own game and play it from start to finish.
days.challenge: Ask two people to play it and write down their feedback.

quiz.q: What is a game design document?
options: A short document that describes your game: goal, controls, rules and win/lose
quiz.explain: A design document is a plan. It says what the game is, how it plays and what counts as winning, before you build it.

quiz.q: Why write the design before building?
options: So you build the right game and do not get lost halfway
quiz.explain: A written plan keeps you focused. Without it, you add random features and never finish.

quiz.q: What makes a game fun to playtest?
options: Clear goals, fair challenges and feedback for every action
quiz.explain: Fun comes from clear goals, fair challenges and instant feedback, not from graphics alone.

project.title: Your Own Game
project.brief: Design and build your own 2D game from scratch: write a one-page design, build at least three levels or a score chase, add sound, particles and a main menu, and playtest it with two people.
checks: A one-page game design exists.
The game has at least three levels or a score chase.
Sound and particles are in the game.
A main menu exists.
Two people playtested the game.
The top problems from playtesting are fixed.

days.title: 2D Lighting and Atmosphere
days.goal: Add light and mood to your game with Unity's 2D lighting.

video.title: Unity for Beginners: Build Your First Game From Zero

steps: Learn what 2D lights do: they brighten parts of the scene and leave others dark.
Add a point light to your player so the area around them glows.
Add a dark ambient light so the level feels moody.
Test the level with and without lights and compare the feeling.
days.task: Add lighting to one level of your game and test how it feels.
days.challenge: Make a torch that flickers by changing the light's intensity over time.

options: It adds light and shadow to a 2D scene, which creates mood and focus
It is a kind of physics
quiz.explain: 2D lights brighten areas and leave others dark, which guides the player's eye and sets the mood.

options: A light that shines in all directions from one point
quiz.explain: A point light glows outward from a spot, like a lamp or a torch.

quiz.q: Why use darkness in a level?
options: Because darkness creates tension and makes the lit areas feel important
quiz.explain: Darkness focuses attention. What is lit matters more, and the unknown feels tense.

days.title: Polishing Your Game
days.goal: Polish your game: fix bugs, improve feel and clean up the menus.

video.title: How to Make a Game! Download and Create New Project

steps: Play your game from start to finish and write down every bug you find.
Fix the three worst bugs.
Improve the game feel: tune jump, speed and enemy behaviour.
Clean up the menus and check all buttons work.
days.task: Fix the top five bugs in your game and improve the feel.
days.challenge: Play the game again and check the fixes worked.

options: Fixing bugs, improving feel and cleaning up the presentation
quiz.explain: Polish is the final pass: bugs fixed, feel tuned, menus clean. It turns a working game into a good one.

quiz.q: Why fix the worst bugs first?
options: Because they block players from finishing the game
quiz.explain: A bug that stops progress matters more than a small visual glitch. Fix blockers first.

quiz.q: How do you know when a game is polished enough?
options: When you can play it start to finish without hitting a bug or a confusing moment
quiz.explain: A game is ready when a new player can finish it without confusion or crashes.

days.title: Building and Publishing Your Game
days.goal: Build your game for PC, WebGL or Android and share it.

video.title: Complete C# Programming

steps: Open Build Settings and pick your target platform.
Build the game and check the output folder.
Run the built game on your computer and check it works.
Upload the WebGL build to itch.io and share the link.
days.task: Build your game and upload it to itch.io.
days.challenge: Share the link with three people and ask them to play it.

options: The finished, playable version of your game for one platform
quiz.explain: A build is your game compiled for a platform, like Windows, WebGL or Android, ready for others to play.

options: A website where indie developers share and sell their games
quiz.explain: itch.io is a marketplace for indie games. You can upload your game there for free and share it.

quiz.q: Why test the built game, not just in the editor?
options: Because the build can behave differently from the editor
quiz.explain: The editor and the build are not identical. Testing the build catches problems players would hit.

days.title: Monetisation and Next Steps
days.goal: Learn how indie games make money and plan your next game.

video.title: How to Make Wall Slide in a 2D Game in Unity for Beginners

steps: Learn the main ways games earn money: selling, ads, in-app purchases and donations.
Learn why most first games should be free: to get players and feedback.
Plan your next game: what you learned, what you would do differently.
Set a goal for the next 30 days of game development.
days.task: Write a plan for your next game with three lessons from this one.
days.challenge: Share your game link in one community and read the feedback.

quiz.q: How do indie games make money?
options: By selling the game, showing ads, selling items inside it, or taking donations
quiz.explain: Indie games earn through sales, ads, in-app purchases or donations. Most use a mix.

quiz.q: Why make your first game free?
options: Because free games get more players and more feedback, which teaches you faster
quiz.explain: A free first game reaches more players. Their feedback teaches you more than a few sales would.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing a game?
options: Share it, read the feedback, and start the next one with what you learned
quiz.explain: Finishing is the start. Sharing brings feedback, and the next game is where the lessons pay off.

days.title: Tilemaps: Building Levels Faster
days.goal: Build levels quickly with tilemaps instead of placing every platform by hand.

video.title: How to make a 2D Game in Unity

steps: Learn what a tilemap is: a grid where you paint tiles to build a level.
Make a tileset from a sprite sheet and add it to a tile palette.
Paint a level with the tilemap: ground, platforms and walls.
Add a Tilemap Collider so the painted tiles are solid.
days.task: Rebuild one of your levels with a tilemap.
days.challenge: Paint a new level in under ten minutes using tiles.

options: A grid-based tool for painting levels from small tiles
quiz.explain: A tilemap is a grid. You paint tiles onto it to build ground, walls and platforms quickly.

quiz.q: Why use tiles instead of placing objects one by one?
options: Because painting is much faster and keeps everything lined up on a grid
quiz.explain: Painting tiles is fast and neat. Placing every platform by hand is slow and uneven.

quiz.q: What does a Tilemap Collider do?
options: It makes the painted tiles solid so the player can stand on them
quiz.explain: A Tilemap Collider turns your painted tiles into a solid surface the player can walk on.

days.title: Enemy AI: Simple Chasing
days.goal: Make an enemy that chases the player when they get close.

video.title: 2D Camera in Unity (Cinemachine Tutorial)

steps: Add a detection range: if the player is within a few metres, chase them.
Move the enemy toward the player while chasing.
Go back to patrolling when the player escapes.
Test the chase and tune the speed so it is fair.
days.task: Add a chasing enemy to your game and test it.
days.challenge: Make the enemy give up the chase after five seconds.

options: The code that decides what an enemy does: patrol, chase, attack
quiz.explain: Enemy AI is the enemy's brain. It decides when to patrol, when to chase and when to attack.

quiz.q: How does an enemy know the player is near?
options: By checking the distance to the player each frame
quiz.explain: The enemy measures the distance to the player. If it is under a set range, it starts chasing.

quiz.q: Why should a chasing enemy be slower than the player?
options: So the player can escape and the game stays fair
quiz.explain: If the enemy is faster, the player can never escape. A slower enemy makes the chase tense but fair.

days.title: Dialogue and Story
days.goal: Add dialogue and a simple story to your game.

video.title: How to Make a Video Game in Unity – Programming (E02)

steps: Write a short story for your game: who is the hero and what do they want?
Add a dialogue box UI that shows one line at a time.
Make an NPC that shows dialogue when the player walks near and presses a key.
Add a typewriter effect that reveals the text letter by letter.
days.task: Add an NPC with three lines of dialogue to your game.
days.challenge: Write an opening line that tells the player their goal.

quiz.q: What is dialogue in a game?
options: Text that characters say, shown in a box on screen
quiz.explain: Dialogue is what characters say. It appears in a box, often one line at a time, while the player reads.

quiz.q: Why add a story to a game?
options: Because a story gives the player a reason to keep playing
quiz.explain: A story gives meaning to the action. Players keep going because they want to know what happens next.

options: Text that appears letter by letter, like someone typing
quiz.explain: A typewriter effect reveals text one letter at a time, which feels alive and keeps the player reading.

days.title: Optimising Performance
days.goal: Keep your game running smoothly on weaker computers.

video.title: Learn C# Beginner FREE Tutorial Course!

steps: Learn what frame rate is and check yours in the Game window.
Find the slowest part: too many sprites, too many lights, or heavy scripts.
Use object pooling for things you create often, like coins or bullets.
Test your game on a weaker computer or with a lower frame rate cap.
days.task: Check your game's frame rate and fix the slowest part.
days.challenge: Replace repeated creating and destroying with object pooling for one thing.

options: How many frames your game draws each second. 60 is smooth, 30 is playable
quiz.explain: Frame rate is frames per second. Higher is smoother. Below 30, the game starts to feel choppy.

options: Reusing objects instead of creating and destroying them again and again
quiz.explain: Pooling keeps a set of ready objects and reuses them, which is faster than creating new ones constantly.

options: So it runs smoothly on more computers and more people can play it
quiz.explain: A game that runs smoothly on weak computers reaches more players. A choppy game drives them away.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Game
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone game and plan your demo.

video.title: COMPLETE COURSE - 2D Game Development in Unity (FREE)

steps: List the games you built and pick the strongest one to finish.
Write a short plan: the game, the levels, the features and the demo.
Practise explaining your game in simple words, as if to a friend.
Record a short video of your game or write a short post showing it.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your game.
days.challenge: Show your game to one person and note their questions, then improve it.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone game?
options: A complete, fun game with a menu, levels, a goal and no crashes
quiz.explain: A good capstone is a complete game: menu, levels, goal, win and lose, and it runs without breaking.

options: Because explaining simply proves you truly understand it
quiz.explain: If you can explain your game in simple words, you really understand it. That is what employers and players look for.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The game, the levels, the features and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the game idea, the levels, the features and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Build and Publish Your Own 2D Game
capstone.brief: Design, build and publish your own complete 2D game in Unity: a clear goal, at least three levels, enemies and collectables, sound and particles, menus and a save system. Publish it on itch.io and share the link with a short demo video.
checks: The game has a clear goal and you can explain it in one sentence.
It has at least three levels or a full score chase.
It has enemies, collectables, a score and health.
It has sound, particles and a main menu.
Progress is saved between sessions.
It is published on itch.io with a playable link.
You can show a live demo and explain how it works in simple words.
deliverables: A published itch.io link to the playable game.
A short demo video or screenshots of the game.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
